entries.note: The design asks for 90ms hover and focus transitions, but the desktop's loop is event-driven and draws nothing when nothing happens. The clock is therefore pull-based: a control asks for its own progress toward a target each frame, the value steps by the elapsed time, and any control still moving sets the animating flag. main.c turns that flag into a 16ms wait and one more frame, so an idle workspace still costs nothing. Slots are a fixed table keyed by microui id with a frame stamp; a control that stops being drawn simply loses its slot to the oldest-stamp victim, which is why no allocation or teardown is needed. A slot created this frame starts at its target rather than at zero, so a control that appears under the pointer does not fade in.

Owned controls draw into the list while the user interface is built, which is right for a workspace that microui then replays over, and wrong for a surface that must sit above every pane. Rather than give the popover a second drawing path, the same primitives record into a fixed buffer between re_ui_overlay_begin and re_ui_overlay_end, and the frame replays them after the panes and the status bar. One buffer, not a stack: spec 080 decision 5 allows one overlay at a time, and the workspace holds a single overlay kind rather than a flag per surface, so "opening one closes the other" is structural instead of a rule to remember. The flush clears the clip when it replayed anything, because a recorded clip would otherwise outlive the frame.

entries.note: These controls draw into the draw list while the UI is being built, whereas microui buffers its own commands and replays them afterwards. Two consequences are load-bearing. First, main.c opens the frame (re_draw_begin) before mu_begin, or the list would be reset after these draws. Second, any microui window that hosts owned controls must carry MU_OPT_NOFRAME and paint its own background through re_ui_panel, because microui's window background would otherwise be replayed on top of them. The toolbar and the pane header follow that rule; pane contents still belong to microui until the views are redrawn.

Owned controls draw straight into the draw list at build time and so never saw microui's clip. Nothing bounded them, and once the explorer and the dashboard could scroll, their rows and path bars painted over the tab strip and the toolbar; the owner reported it as content drawn above its pane. Every control now takes its container's clip before drawing, the primitives emit it lazily so an unchanged clip costs nothing, and a control that narrows its own clip intersects with the container's rather than replacing it. A panel or a popover clears the scissor instead, because both are drawn outside any container and the popover's shadow deliberately reaches past its window. The regression test is in orchestrator/tests/native-scrollbars.spec.mjs: it samples every row of the toolbar and the tab strip, scrolls the explorer and requires that no pixel above the pane changed.

entries.note: The menus card fills a hovered row with the accent and flips its text to the on-accent ink, rather than tinting a selection colour. The icon, the check mark and the keyboard hint follow the same ink past the halfway point of the transition, so a row never shows accent-coloured glyphs on an accent ground. The hint is drawn in the mono face at the small size, as the card does, and is right-aligned by measurement rather than by a reserved column, so a row without a hint has no gap.

The accent hue is the one token a person moves at runtime, and this is the only place a gradient appears (spec 076 decision 7, spec 080). The track is twelve ramps between neighbouring hues rather than one two-stop gradient, because a hue wheel is not a straight line in any colour space; twelve segments keep the error under a shade while staying twelve commands. Each stop comes from re_theme_swatch, which is the preset's own accent lightness and chroma at that hue, so the colour under the thumb is literally the accent the workspace will take. Only the first and last segments round their outer corners, which is what makes the strip read as one pill.
